title: Episode 114: Thomas Jefferson and the Lewis and Clark Expedition: The Corps of Discovery
description:
In 1804, President Thomas Jefferson dispatched Captain Meriwether Lewis, William Clark, and the Corps of Discovery on an epic 8,000-mile scientific expedition across the newly acquired Louisiana territory, reaching the Pacific Ocean and mapping a continent.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the visionary mind of our third President, Thomas Jefferson, during the breathtaking spring of eighteen oh-four, to witness one of the greatest epics of scientific exploration and human endurance in world history: the Lewis and Clark Expedition. Having purchased eight hundred and twenty-eight thousand square miles of uncharted wilderness from Napoleon Bonaparte in the Louisiana Purchase, Jefferson envisioned an American empire of liberty stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific. To explore this mysterious, unmapped continent, Jefferson selected his brilliant twenty-eight-year-old personal secretary, Captain Meriwether Lewis, and frontiersman William Clark. Leading thirty-three soldiers, a Newfoundland dog named Seaman, and an enslaved man named York—joined along the trail by a courageous Shoshone teenager named Sacagawea—the Corps of Discovery journeyed eight thousand miles into the unknown. Here is George with the full, magnificent chronicle.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: JEFFERSON'S VISION OF AN EMPIRE OF LIBERTY
Long before he became President of the United States, Thomas Jefferson was obsessed with the mysteries of the vast, unmapped trans-Mississippi West. Sitting in his magnificent neoclassical library at Monticello, surrounded by thousands of scientific treatises, geographical maps, and botanical specimens, Jefferson looked westward with romantic, scientific fascination. In eighteen oh-three, virtually nothing was known of the vast wilderness stretching from the Mississippi River to the Pacific Ocean. Contemporary European maps showed empty spaces labeled 'Terra Incognita,' while Enlightenment scientists debated whether prehistoric woolly mammoths, giant ground sloths, mountains of pure rock salt, and active volcanoes still existed in the interior.
Then, in the spring of eighteen oh-three, came the geopolitical coup of the century: the Louisiana Purchase. Seizing upon Napoleon Bonaparte's desperation for cash following a catastrophic slave rebellion in Haiti, Jefferson's diplomats purchased eight hundred and twenty-eight thousand square miles of land from France for fifteen million dollars—doubling the territorial size of the United States overnight for less than three cents an acre.
Jefferson envisioned this immense continent as an 'empire of liberty' that would provide independent farmland for generations of free American yeoman farmers. But the land was completely uncharted. Even more pressing was the race for commercial empire: British fur traders from the North West Company were already pushing across western Canada, and imperial Spain held California and the Southwest. Jefferson resolved to launch a bold, scientific transcontinental expedition to find a practical water route to the Pacific—the legendary Northwest Passage—and document the geography, native nations, flora, and fauna of the American continent.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: LEWIS, CLARK, AND THE CORPS OF DISCOVERY
To lead this unprecedented expedition, President Jefferson selected a man he knew and trusted intimately: twenty-eight-year-old Captain Meriwether Lewis. Lewis was a Virginia aristocrat, veteran frontier army officer, and had served for two years as Jefferson's private secretary in the White House. Jefferson personally tutored Lewis in botany, zoology, and geography, sending him to Philadelphia to study celestial navigation, astronomy, and medicine under the nation's preeminent scientists, including Dr. Benjamin Rush.
Recognizing the monumental perils of the journey, Lewis insisted on recruiting a co-commander: his trusted former army comrade, thirty-three-year-old William Clark. Clark was a seasoned frontier soldier, expert cartographer, and river navigator whose steady, calm temperament perfectly complemented Lewis's brilliant but moody, introspective nature. Although the War Department refused to grant Clark an official captain's commission, Lewis refused to acknowledge the slight, treating Clark as a full, equal co-captain throughout the entire journey.
Together, they assembled an elite, handpicked strike force of thirty-three men known as the Corps of Discovery: skilled backwoodsmen, hunters, carpenters, blacksmiths, and soldiers. The party included Clark's enslaved Black companion, York, an imposing, athletic man who proved an indispensable scout and hunter, and Lewis's massive one-hundred-and-fifty-pound black Newfoundland dog, Seaman. Outfitted with fifty-five-foot keelboat, two wooden pirogues, scientific instruments, twenty-one bales of trade gifts for native tribes, and modern Harper's Ferry flintlock rifles, the expedition assembled near St. Louis during the winter of eighteen oh-three.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: UP THE MIGHTY MISSOURI
On Monday afternoon, May fourteenth, eighteen oh-four, the Corps of Discovery shoved off from Camp Dubois into the murky, swirling current of the Missouri River. Ahead lay two thousand miles of grueling upstream navigation against one of the most treacherous, powerful rivers on earth. Known as the 'Big Muddy,' the Missouri was a churning obstacle course of collapsing mud cutbanks, submerged tree snags known as sawyers, and powerful whirlpools that constantly threatened to splinter the wooden keelboat.
For five grueling months, the men pulled the heavy boat upriver using sixty-foot tow ropes while wading waist-deep in freezing mud, poling against the rocky riverbed, and battling suffocating clouds of mosquitoes and gnats. Lewis walked the shoreline, filling his leather-bound journals with meticulous scientific descriptions and sketches of new species never before seen by science: coyotes, pronghorn antelopes, prairie dogs, and the terrifying grizzly bear, which took multiple rifle balls to bring down.
In late October eighteen oh-four, sixteen hundred miles upriver in modern-day North Dakota, the expedition arrived at the massive earth-lodge villages of the Mandan and Hidatsa nations. Home to five thousand people, these thriving agricultural trading hubs were more populous than Washington, D.C. There, the explorers constructed a triangular log fortress named Fort Mandan, settling in for a brutal northern plains winter where temperatures plummeted to forty-five degrees below zero.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: SACAGAWEA AND THE GREAT UNKNOWN
At Fort Mandan, Lewis and Clark made the most crucial personnel acquisition of the entire expedition. They hired Toussaint Charbonneau, an eccentric French-Canadian fur trapper, as an interpreter. Charbonneau's teenage Shoshone wife, Sacagawea, was approximately sixteen years old, pregnant, and had been captured from her native Rocky Mountain homeland by a Hidatsa raiding party years earlier.
In February eighteen oh-five, inside the drafty fort, Sacagawea endured a difficult, agonizing labor. Lewis administered a traditional folk remedy—powdered rattlesnake rattles dissolved in water—and she safely delivered a healthy baby boy named Jean Baptiste, affectionately nicknamed 'Pompey' by Clark. When the expedition departed Fort Mandan in April eighteen oh-five in six small dugout canoes, Sacagawea strapped her two-month-old infant to her back and joined the voyage.
Sacagawea proved to be the salvation of the expedition. As the only woman in the party, her presence was an unmistakable white flag of peace: war parties never traveled with women and nursing infants, signaling to hostile tribes that the Americans came in peace. She foraged for edible wild licorice, wild artichokes, and prairie turnips, keeping the men alive during times of starvation, and recognized geographic landmarks from her childhood that guided the captains toward the Rocky Mountains.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GREAT FALLS AND THE SHOSHONE REUNION
In June eighteen oh-five, the expedition encountered one of the most formidable obstacles of the journey: the Great Falls of the Missouri in modern-day Montana. Instead of a single waterfall, they were confronted with five colossal cataracts tumbling across eighteen miles of rugged canyons. In an epic eighteen-day ordeal of grueling physical labor, the men constructed crude wooden wagons with wheels cut from cottonwood trunks, hauling eight tons of baggage and heavy dugout canoes overland across rough terrain blanketed in prickly pear cactus, braving violent hailstorms and grizzly bear attacks.
Reaching the headwaters of the Missouri, Lewis walked ahead of the canoes across the continental divide at Lemhi Pass, expecting to look down upon a gentle, rolling river valley leading smoothly to the Pacific Ocean—the Northwest Passage that Jefferson had dreamt of. Instead, Lewis stood atop the ridge in stunned silence: stretching out to the horizon as far as the eye could see were endless, snow-capped jagged mountain ranges. There was no water route. The continent was far wider and more formidable than anyone in Europe or America had ever imagined.
Desperately needing horses to cross the towering mountains before winter blizzards trapped them, Lewis made contact with a band of Shoshone warriors under Chief Cameahwait. When Sacagawea was brought into the council lodge to interpret, she looked across the buffalo robes at the chief, let out a piercing cry, and rushed across the circle to embrace him with tears streaming down her face: Chief Cameahwait was her beloved biological older brother, whom she had not seen since her capture five years earlier. Overwhelmed by joy, Cameahwait provided the expedition with twenty-nine horses and expert mountain guides.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BITTERROOT STARVATION AND THE PACIFIC OCEAN
In September eighteen oh-five, guided by an elder Shoshone named Old Toby, the Corps of Discovery plunged into the Bitterroot Mountains along the Lolo Trail. What followed was a eleven-day nightmare of freezing starvation. Early blizzards wiped out the mountain trail, game disappeared completely from the sub-alpine forests, and the men were reduced to killing and eating several of their pack horses and melting snow for water to survive.
Stumbling out of the mountains half-dead from starvation and dysentery onto the Weippe Prairie in Idaho, they were saved by the hospitable Nez Perce nation, who fed them dried salmon and camas roots. Reaching the Clearwater and Columbia rivers, the explorers carved fresh dugout canoes from ponderosa pines and rode the rushing rapids toward the ocean.
On November seventh, eighteen oh-five, paddling through dense coastal fog and heavy rain swells near the mouth of the Columbia River, William Clark wrote the ecstatic, immortal lines in his field journal: 'Ocian in view! O! the joy!' Nine days later, the expedition reached the open Pacific Ocean at Cape Disappointment. Before constructing their winter quarters at Fort Clatsop, Lewis and Clark held a historic democratic vote to decide where to build the fort: every member of the party was given an equal vote, marking the first time in American history that an enslaved Black man and an Indigenous woman cast ballots alongside white citizens.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE RETURN AND THE LEGACY OF THE CORPS
After enduring a miserable, rain-soaked winter at Fort Clatsop, where it rained all but twelve days of their three-month stay, the Corps of Discovery commenced their four-thousand-mile return journey in March eighteen oh-six. Splitting into separate exploring parties to map the Marias and Yellowstone rivers, they reunited on the Missouri and swept downstream with the current.
On September twenty-third, eighteen oh-six, two years, four months, and nine days after they had set out, thirty-three sun-blackened, buckskin-clad men paddled their canoes into the harbor of St. Louis. The entire nation had long given them up for dead. Church bells rang across the city, crowds lined the riverbanks, and news of their miraculous return was rushed by express courier to President Jefferson in Washington.
The achievements of the Lewis and Clark Expedition were staggering beyond measure. In over eight thousand miles of travel through uncharted wilderness, the expedition had lost only one single man—Sergeant Charles Floyd, who tragically died of a burst appendix early in the journey. Clark's monumental master map of the American West completely revolutionized world cartography, tracing the true continental spine of the Rocky Mountains and the course of the Columbia River.
Lewis filled scientific journals with descriptions of one hundred and seventy-eight new plant species and one hundred and twenty-two animal species previously unknown to science. Most importantly, the Corps of Discovery opened the American continent, turning Thomas Jefferson's dream of a continental republic into an enduring geographic reality. Today, the trail of the Corps of Discovery remains a sacred journey in the American imagination: an epic testament to human curiosity, cooperation, and the boundless wonder of the uncharted earth.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Lewis and Clark Expedition opened the American West, transforming Thomas Jefferson's continental vision into a living reality. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we continue with our second Thomas Jefferson story: the dramatic confrontation with the Barbary Pirates on the shores of Tripoli.
